summary: Describes security threats for larger multicast routing infrastructures, within or between domains. It analyzes PIM-SM in its main operational modes, including any-source and source-specific multicast, and suggests enhancements. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Multicast sends one stream to many people. This lists ways someone could mess with it and what can be done.

subtitle: How to defend multicast routing from denial-of-service attacks

tldr.problem: PIM-SM (Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode) multicast routing can be abused to launch denial-of-service attacks by flooding joins to non-existent groups, sending data to empty groups, or disrupting existing multicast streams.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs attack types affecting routers and rendezvous points, analyzes vulnerabilities in ASM, SSM, and Embedded-RP models, and proposes defensive mechanisms such as rate-limiting at designated routers and rendezvous points, remote routability checks, and passive PIM modes.
tldr.outcome: Implementation of these protections can significantly reduce attack surfaces, though no single solution addresses all threats across all deployment models.

today: RFC 4609 is an Informational RFC published in August 2006. PIM-SM remains widely deployed, and these security considerations continue to be relevant. Most modern deployments either use SSM (which provides better inherent security) or implement the rate-limiting and remote routability mechanisms described here.

sections.title: PIM-SM and Its Attack Surface
sections.content:
Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) is a scalable multicast routing protocol for scenarios where few senders and receivers are active. It uses a central Rendezvous Point (RP) to discover sources and build multicast distribution trees.

PIM-SM operates in three main modes: traditional Any-Source Multicast (ASM), where receivers can join any group and discover any sender; Source-Specific Multicast (SSM), where receivers explicitly request traffic from a specific source; and Embedded-RP, a variant of ASM that encodes the RP address in the group address.

This memo focuses on attack threats to large multicast routing networks, specifically attacks that exploit the multicast routing infrastructure itself rather than on-link attacks or end-to-end payload security.
sections.eli5: PIM-SM lets many people listen to one sender's broadcast. Attackers can trick routers by pretending to be listeners, or by sending fake data, overloading the network.

sections.title: Types of Multicast Attacks
sections.content:
Receiver-based attacks, or join flooding, occur when a host rapidly joins many different multicast groups or source-specific channels that may or may not exist. Each join causes the Designated Router (DR) to send a PIM Join message upstream, creating multicast state (routing table entries) in routers along the path. State in PIM lasts 260 seconds by default, even if no actual traffic arrives. A single host generating 100 joins per second with 10 sources each can create 260,000 state entries within 260 seconds, overwhelming routers.

Source-based attacks include data flooding, where a host sends multicast packets to groups with no real receivers, forcing routers to process and encapsulate or forward unwanted traffic. This wastes CPU and memory. A second source-based threat is group integrity violation: a malicious source sends traffic to an existing group, disrupting legitimate users. This is particularly dangerous with ASM and Embedded-RP, where sources are discovered through an RP, allowing arbitrary injection of unwanted content.

Two aggravating factors amplify these attacks: distant RP/source problem, where non-existent RPs or sources cause state to persist across many routers because PIM has no way to verify addresses are routable, and lack of receiver information in PIM Joins, which prevents routers from enforcing policies about who can receive multicast.
sections.eli5: Attackers ask to join millions of fake groups (flooding the router's memory), send garbage data that fills pipes (flooding the CPU), or trick users by sending bad data to real groups. All three waste resources.

sections.title: Threat Comparison Across Models
sections.content:
The three operational modes have different security characteristics:

ASM (Any-Source Multicast): Poor resistance to forged joins and very poor resistance to malicious sources. An attacker can inject traffic to any group with few barriers. The Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) used for inter-domain source discovery amplifies attacks by flooding information about malicious sources across the entire Internet.

SSM (Source-Specific Multicast): Better security than ASM. Receivers explicitly specify which source they want, preventing unknown sources from injecting traffic. However, forged joins still create state, and an attacker who can spoof a source address (by running on the same link as the real source) can still inject traffic.

Embedded-RP: Offers moderate protection by embedding the RP address in the group address itself. This prevents arbitrary RP addresses from being used, but still allows forged joins and, in some cases, source spoofing attacks.
sections.eli5: ASM is weakest (anyone can send to any group). SSM is stronger (only the real source can send). Embedded-RP is in between (RP is baked into the group address).

sections.title: Rate-Limiting and Defensive Mechanisms
sections.content:
The RFC proposes several rate-limiting approaches to mitigate attacks:

Group Management Protocol (IGMP/MLD) rate-limiters at the DR limit the rate at which hosts can join groups (e.g., 1 join per second). This stops join flooding at the source.

Source transmission rate-limiters restrict multicast data transmission from a link (e.g., 10 packets per second), defending against data flooding.

PIM signalling rate-limiters limit all PIM control messages on the router, providing second-order defense if IGMP limits are not implemented or fail.

Register decapsulation rate-limiters at the RP restrict how many encapsulated packets are processed per second, protecting the RP from CPU exhaustion.

MSDP source-active rate-limiters prevent a single source from advertising too many groups, limiting MSDP state explosions.

Remote routability signalling involves checking whether an RP or source address is actually reachable before establishing state. Approaches include stopping Register messages if ICMP unreachable is received, using timers to expire unacknowledged registrations, or performing return routability checks (sending a probe to the RP and requiring a response before sending Register messages).

Passive PIM mode allows stub networks to receive multicast without running the PIM protocol on the link itself, preventing hosts from disrupting routers with false PIM messages.
sections.eli5: Rate-limiters are speed bumps: slow down joins, slow down data, slow down PIM messages. Check that addresses are real before trusting them. Let hosts receive without running PIM.

sections.title: Practical Implementation and Limitations
sections.content:
Rate-limiting works best when deployed at the edge of the network (DRs), catching attacks before they propagate. However, hosts aware of rate-limiters can circumvent them by generating PIM messages directly instead of relying on group management protocols. Protection at domain borders (RPs and MSDP peers) provides a second layer of defense against attacks that escape the edge.

Legitimate users can be harmed by rate-limiters if an attacker shares the same link; for example, if rate-limiting is per-interface, a legitimate user on the same link as an attacker may be unable to join groups. White-listing (excluding known legitimate sources from rate limit counting) can mitigate this.

Authentication and cryptography are mentioned but not specified in depth in this memo. The PIM specification itself allows IPsec for authenticating Register messages and establishing PIM adjacencies, which would help verify that routers are genuinely authorized to send control messages. However, authentication alone is insufficient against worms or compromised hosts that can generate valid cryptographic signatures.

The memo notes that ASM's global MSDP flooding is the most serious threat today, while SSM with proper implementation provides significantly better security properties for most deployments.
sections.eli5: Rate-limiters work best at the edge. Bad guys can trick them. It's hard to let good users through while blocking bad guys on the same link. IPsec helps but won't stop a virus on a good computer.
